couplr

matching two groups into pairs

couplr pairs the units of two groups, such as treated and control patients, plots, sites or samples, so that the total covariate distance over all pairs is as small as possible.

The pairing is a linear assignment problem: the distances between every unit of one group and every unit of the other form a cost matrix, and the solver picks one partner per unit so that the summed distance is minimal. couplr solves it exactly in C++, by default with the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm, so the total distance is the global minimum and a solve can be certified optimal. You then check covariate balance on the matched pairs and decide whether to use them as they are or to tighten the match with calipers and blocks.

couplr supports:

  • Large pools. memory_mode = "lazy" computes each distance when the solver needs it, and memory_mode = "implicit" generates only the pairs the optimum needs, so neither builds the full distance matrix.
  • Constraints and strata. Calipers, a maximum distance, matching within blocks and several controls per treated unit are arguments of match_couples().
  • Other matching designs. Full matching, coarsened exact matching, cardinality matching, propensity score subclassification and propensity score matching take the same two-group input and return results the diagnostics understand.
  • Balance and sensitivity. balance_diagnostics() reports standardized differences, variance ratios and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, and sensitivity_analysis() computes Rosenbaum bounds for unmeasured confounding.
  • Analysis with other matching packages. as_matchit() converts a result to a MatchIt object, so cobalt balance tables and marginaleffects estimates run on it.
  • The assignment solvers. lap_solve() takes a cost matrix directly and offers nineteen solvers by name, the k best assignments and batches of independent problems.

The solve has no random seed: the same input gives the same pairing on every run. When several pairings tie at the minimum, which one comes back can depend on the order of the rows. Comparison with Alternatives sets couplr beside MatchIt, optmatch and designmatch.

Installation

Install the released version from CRAN. Windows and macOS get a binary package and need no build tools:

install.packages("couplr")

The development version compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools matching your R version
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install couplr from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/couplr")

The C++ code needs a compiler that supports C++17. It links only to Rcpp, which is installed from CRAN with the package, and needs no system libraries.

Usage

  1. Match the two groups with match_couples().
  2. Check covariate balance with balance_diagnostics().
  3. Join the pairs to their covariates with join_matched() for the analysis.

The input is two data frames, one row per unit, each with an identifier column (id by default) and the covariates named in vars. auto_scale = TRUE puts covariates measured in different units on a common scale before the distances are computed.

library(couplr)

set.seed(1)
treated <- data.frame(
  id = 1:6,
  age = round(rnorm(6, 45, 10)),
  income = round(rnorm(6, 55, 12))
)
control <- data.frame(
  id = 1:12,
  age = round(rnorm(12, 50, 12)),
  income = round(rnorm(12, 48, 15))
)

vars <- c("age", "income")
result <- match_couples(treated, control, vars = vars, auto_scale = TRUE)
#> Auto-selected scaling method: standardize
result
#> couplr result: one-to-one matching, optimal
#>   Left units:         6 matched of 6
#>   Right units:        6 matched of 12
#>   Pairs:              6
#>   Total distance:     6.44862

Each of the six treated units has one control partner, and six controls stay unmatched. Balance is checked on the matched pairs:

bal <- balance_diagnostics(result, treated, control, vars = vars)
bal

join_matched() returns one row per pair, with the covariates of both partners and their differences:

paired <- join_matched(result, treated, control)
paired
#> # A tibble: 6 × 10
#>   pair_id left_id right_id distance .age_diff .income_diff age_left income_left
#>     <int>   <int>    <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1       1       1        1    0.453        -4            4       39          61
#> 2       2       2        9    1.39        -14           10       47          64
#> 3       3       3        2    1.64         14           15       37          62
#> 4       4       4        6    0.236         0           -3       61          51
#> 5       5       5        7    1.06        -12            5       48          73
#> 6       6       6       12    1.67         11           18       37          60
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: age_right <dbl>, income_right <dbl>

Matching large pools

The exact solve applies to large pools as well. memory_mode = "implicit" generates candidate pairs in rounds and stops when the optimum needs no more of them; method = "greedy" gives up the optimality guarantee for speed and keeps the same scaling, constraints and blocking:

match_couples(treated, control, vars = vars, memory_mode = "implicit")
match_couples(treated, control, vars = vars, method = "greedy")

Matching Workflows compares optimal and greedy matching and the greedy strategies.

Scaling and constraints

scale chooses how covariates are scaled ("standardize", "range" or "robust"). max_distance forbids pairs beyond a covariate distance, calipers sets a maximum absolute difference per variable, block_id names a column to match within, and ratio sets the number of controls per treated unit:

match_couples(
  treated, control,
  vars = vars,
  scale = "robust",
  max_distance = 2,
  calipers = list(age = 5),
  ratio = 2
)

Treated units without a partner inside the constraints stay unmatched, and the printed result counts them.

Other matching designs

full_match() forms groups of variable size in which every unit is used, cem_match() matches exactly on coarsened covariates, and cardinality_match() maximizes the number of matched pairs subject to balance constraints:

full_match(treated, control, vars = vars)
cem_match(treated, control, vars = vars)
cardinality_match(treated, control, vars = vars)

ps_match() and subclass_match() take a formula of the treatment indicator on the covariates and a single data frame. sensitivity_analysis() takes the name of an outcome column and reports Rosenbaum bounds over a range of the sensitivity parameter gamma.

The assignment solvers

lap_solve() takes a cost matrix, including rectangular ones and forbidden pairs (NA or Inf). method = "auto" enumerates problems up to 8 by 8, uses Hopcroft-Karp when the finite costs are all equal or all 0 or 1, and uses Jonker-Volgenant otherwise:

cost <- matrix(c(4, 2, 8, 4, 3, 7, 3, 1, 6), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

lap_solve(cost)
lap_solve(cost, method = "hungarian")
lap_solve_kbest(cost, k = 3)

lap_solvers() lists the nineteen solvers with their references, among them Hungarian, Kuhn-Munkres, Bertsekas auction, Goldberg-Kennedy cost scaling, Gabow-Tarjan bit scaling, push-relabel and network simplex. bottleneck_assignment() minimizes the largest cost instead of the total, and sinkhorn() returns an entropy-regularized transport plan. The Algorithm Collection describes each solver.

pixel_morph() treats two images as source and target pixel sets and morphs one into the other along the optimal assignment, which shows a solve as an animation.
